reason: The sources provide 12 distinct matching claims regarding the discovery, location, and physical scale of the NGC 206 star cloud.
story: NGC 206 is a gargantuan star cloud located over two million light-years away in the Andromeda Galaxy. Discovered by William Herschel in 1786, this colossal nursery is so enormous that it was clearly visible to 18th-century astronomers across the vast intergalactic void. While most distant objects look like tiny pinpricks, NGC 206 is a physically extended region of star formation, recognized today as one of the most prominent features in our nearest neighbor galaxy. It was originally cataloged as a faint, milky nebulosity and later included in the New General Catalogue. Astronomers like John Herschel mapped its large scale, though early instruments struggled to resolve its individual stars. Today, we know it as a massive engine of stellar birth situated within Andromeda's spiral arms, a cosmic landmark so massive it allows us to witness the structural details of another galaxy from Earth.
angle: NGC 206 is a star-forming region so colossal that it appears as a distinct, extended structure within the Andromeda Galaxy, visible from Earth across 2.5 million light-years.

claims.claim: The object is identified as NGC 206.
It is located within the Andromeda Galaxy.
The Andromeda Galaxy is also known as M31.
It was discovered by the astronomer William Herschel.
The official discovery date is October 17, 1786.
It is classified as a star cloud.
It is a known star-forming region.
John Herschel also observed the object in the 19th century.
Historical descriptions label the object as very large.
The object has a visually extended shape rather than a point-like appearance.
It is physically a part of the Andromeda Galaxy rather than an independent galaxy.
It is included in the New General Catalogue.

disputed: Brightness: Wikipedia describes it as the brightest star cloud in Andromeda, but Dreyer's NGC notes describe it as very faint; attribute as a conspicuous but challenging target for early telescopes.
Discovery date: Wikipedia mentions a possible 1784 observation, while Seligman only confirms 1786; attribute the 1784 date as a possibility.
Orientation: Wikipedia notes it as horizontal, while Dreyer's entry describes it as extended north-south; the script should avoid specifying a specific axis.
